# Device for Controlling and Measuring Welding Defects on Cylindrical Walls

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to a device (3) designed for the control and measurement of welding defects present on cylindrical walls, such as those encountered in a "vessel bottom penetration" wall within a nuclear reactor. This device addresses the critical need for precise, non-destructive testing methods capable of detecting and characterizing defects in weld structures that are essential to the safety and integrity of nuclear reactor components.

## General Structure of the Device

The device comprises a control head (4) that functions as a probe, structured along a longitudinal axis extending between a proximal end and a distal end. This elongated configuration allows the control head to be inserted and maneuvered within the confined spaces typical of nuclear reactor vessel penetrations, enabling access to the weld areas requiring inspection.

## Configuration of the Control Head

The control head (4) is characterized by two distinct and functionally opposed sides:

### First Side: The Inner Surface

The control head features a first side, designated as the "inner" side (42), which is equipped with at least one ultrasonic wave translator. This translator serves as the primary sensing element responsible for the detection of welding defects through the emission and reception of ultrasonic waves, exploiting the well-established principles of ultrasonic non-destructive testing to identify anomalies such as cracks, porosities, or incomplete fusion within the weld structure.

### Second Side: The Outer Surface

Opposite to the inner side, the control head presents a second side, referred to as the "outer" side (43). This outer side is distinguished by a curved surface shaped as a fraction of a cylinder, exhibiting a convexity that faces outward. Notably, this cylindrical fraction shares a longitudinal axis that runs parallel to the longitudinal axis of the control head itself, ensuring geometric coherence between the overall probe structure and its outer contact surface. This convex configuration is particularly advantageous for facilitating smooth contact and controlled displacement of the device along the cylindrical wall being inspected.

## Configuration of the Wave Translator

The ultrasonic wave translator itself is composed of a series (5) of adjacent elements, each of which is configured to operate dually as both an emitter and a receiver of ultrasonic waves. This dual functionality allows each element to both generate the ultrasonic signal directed toward the material under inspection and subsequently capture the returning echo signals that carry information about internal defects.

These adjacent elements are arranged so as to collectively form a curved cylindrical fraction, but in this instance, the fraction is oriented with a concavity facing outward—that is, opposite in orientation to the convex outer side of the control head. This cylindrical arrangement of the translator elements is likewise aligned along the same longitudinal axis as the control head, maintaining overall structural and functional coherence throughout the device.

## Geometric Relationship Between the Two Surfaces

A key inventive feature of this device lies in the specific geometric relationship established between the outer side and the wave translator arrangement. Each of these two curved surfaces—the convex cylindrical fraction of the outer side (43) and the concave cylindrical fraction formed by the translator elements (5)—is bounded by end generatrices, which define planes at their respective extremities.

According to the invention, these planes containing the end generatrices of the outer side's cylindrical fraction and of the wave translator's cylindrical fraction are configured such that they form a non-null acute angle (β) between them. This deliberate angular offset defines a specific and precise geometric relationship within the device, distinguishing it from configurations in which the two cylindrical fractions would be coaxially aligned without angular displacement. This angular relationship (β) is instrumental in optimizing the positioning and orientation of the ultrasonic wave translator relative to the contact surface of the device, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of defect detection along curved welding surfaces such as those found in vessel bottom penetrations of nuclear reactors.

# Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to the field of non-destructive testing (NDT) of metallic components, and more particularly to ultrasonic inspection devices designed for detecting welding defects on cylindrical or curved surfaces. The invention finds particular application in the nuclear industry, where the integrity of welded joints on pressure vessels—such as the bottom head penetrations of nuclear reactor vessels—must be verified with extremely high reliability throughout the operational life of the plant.

# Background of the Invention

Nuclear reactor pressure vessels incorporate numerous penetrations through their bottom heads to accommodate instrumentation tubes, control rod drive mechanisms, and other components essential to reactor operation. These penetrations are typically welded to the vessel wall using techniques such as J-groove or partial penetration welds. Because these welds are subjected to high temperatures, high pressures, and significant mechanical and thermal cycling over decades of service, they are susceptible to degradation mechanisms including primary water stress corrosion cracking (PWSCC), fatigue cracking, and other forms of weld defects.

Detecting such defects at an early stage is critical to ensuring the continued safe operation of the reactor and to preventing costly unplanned outages or, in the worst case, loss of coolant accidents. Ultrasonic testing (UT) has long been established as one of the most effective methods for detecting subsurface flaws in metallic welds, as it allows for volumetric inspection without damaging the component under test.

However, conventional ultrasonic probes, which are typically designed with flat contact surfaces, present significant limitations when applied to curved geometries such as the cylindrical walls of vessel bottom penetrations. A flat probe placed against a curved surface creates uneven contact, air gaps, and inconsistent coupling between the transducer elements and the material being inspected. This results in signal loss, poor beam focusing, and reduced sensitivity to small defects—precisely the type of flaws that must be detected in safety-critical nuclear components. Furthermore, existing curved probes, when available, are often custom-manufactured for a single radius of curvature, making them impractical for inspecting vessels or penetrations with varying diameters.

There therefore exists a need for an ultrasonic inspection device capable of maintaining reliable acoustic coupling with cylindrical surfaces of varying curvature, while simultaneously providing precise control over the transmission and reception of ultrasonic waves so as to maximize defect detection sensitivity.

# Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides a control head, or probe device, specifically adapted for the ultrasonic inspection of welding defects on cylindrical walls, including but not limited to the bottom penetrations of nuclear reactor vessels. The device is characterized by a dual-surface construction in which the inner side of the probe—the side intended to make contact with, or be positioned adjacent to, the component under inspection—comprises an array of ultrasonic emitter-receiver elements arranged side by side along a concave cylindrical surface. This concave configuration is specifically shaped to conform to the convex outer or inner surface of the cylindrical component being tested, such as the tube or nozzle forming the vessel penetration.

In contrast, the outer side of the probe—the side facing away from the inspected component—is formed with a convex cylindrical surface. This outer surface may, for example, serve as an interface for mounting the probe onto a manipulator, scanning fixture, or robotic delivery system used to position the probe accurately relative to the weld under inspection.

A key inventive feature of the device lies in the geometric relationship between the concave inner surface and the convex outer surface: the respective planes of curvature of these two surfaces are arranged so as to form a non-zero acute angle relative to one another, rather than being parallel or coincident as in conventional probe designs. This angular offset between the two curved surfaces enables the ultrasonic emitter-receiver elements to be oriented in a manner that optimizes the angle of incidence of the ultrasonic beam relative to the weld geometry, thereby improving the probability of detecting defects oriented in various directions within the weld, including both circumferentially and axially oriented flaws.

# Detailed Description

## Structure of the Control Head

In accordance with a preferred embodiment, the control head comprises a body, typically formed from a rigid or semi-rigid material such as a machined polymer, composite, or metal alloy suitable for use in the ambient conditions of the inspection environment (including, where applicable, elevated temperatures or radiation fields encountered in nuclear facilities).

The inner side of the body is machined or molded to form a concave cylindrical surface, the radius of curvature of which is selected to substantially match the outer or inner radius of the cylindrical component to be inspected—for example, the tube forming a vessel bottom penetration. Distributed along this concave surface is a plurality of ultrasonic transducer elements, arranged edge-to-edge or in closely spaced adjacent positions, so as to form a continuous or quasi-continuous array. Each element is capable of functioning both as an emitter, generating ultrasonic pulses that propagate into the component under test, and as a receiver, capturing the reflected or transmitted ultrasonic signals resulting from interaction with internal defects, geometric features, or the back wall of the component.

The adjacent arrangement of the transducer elements allows the device to function similarly to a phased-array probe, wherein individual elements can be selectively activated, or activated in a coordinated sequence with controlled time delays, to steer or focus the resulting ultrasonic beam electronically. This permits inspection of multiple regions of the weld without requiring physical repositioning of the probe, and further allows for beam angles to be adjusted dynamically to interrogate defects of different orientations.

## The Convex Outer Surface and the Angular Offset

On the opposite side of the control head, the outer surface is formed with a convex cylindrical profile. This surface may serve multiple functional purposes, including providing a mounting interface compatible with cylindrical guide rails, robotic arms, or other delivery mechanisms used to position the probe within confined or difficult-to-access regions, such as the underside of a reactor pressure vessel.

The defining structural feature of the invention is that the plane defined by the curvature of the inner concave surface and the plane defined by the curvature of the outer convex surface are not parallel, but rather intersect at a non-zero acute angle. This angular relationship means that the axis of curvature of the transducer array (inner surface) is tilted with respect to the axis of curvature of the mounting or support surface (outer surface).

This deliberate angular offset provides several technical advantages. First, it allows the transducer array to be oriented at an optimal angle relative to the weld bevel or fusion line, even when the mounting structure supporting the probe must be aligned along a different axis dictated by mechanical or access constraints. Second, it enables the ultrasonic beams generated by the emitter-receiver elements to be directed toward the weld root, sidewalls, or heat-affected zone at incidence angles calculated to maximize reflection from defects such as cracks, lack of fusion, or porosity, which may not be efficiently detected using a purely parallel or coaxial arrangement of the two surfaces. Third, the offset angle facilitates a more compact overall probe design, allowing the device to be inserted into narrow annular spaces, such as those found between a vessel penetration tube and surrounding structures.

## Operation of the Device

In use, the control head is positioned so that its concave inner surface is brought into acoustic contact—either directly or through a coupling medium such as water or gel—with the cylindrical outer or inner wall of the component under inspection. The convex outer surface remains engaged with the supporting manipulator or scanning apparatus, which may translate or rotate the probe along the length or circumference of the component to achieve full coverage of the weld region.

During operation, the array of emitter-receiver elements is activated according to a predetermined firing sequence, which may be controlled by an external ultrasonic pulser-receiver unit and associated phased-array electronics. Ultrasonic pulses generated by the elements propagate through the coupling medium and into the wall of the component, where they interact with the weld structure. Reflected signals resulting from internal defects, geometric discontinuities, or the opposite wall surface are captured by the same or adjacent elements and processed to generate defect indications, which may be displayed as A-scans, B-scans, or C-scans for interpretation by inspection personnel or automated defect recognition software.

Because the transducer elements are arranged along a curvature that closely matches that of the inspected component, acoustic coupling is significantly improved relative to flat probes, minimizing signal attenuation due to air gaps and ensuring more uniform beam propagation into the material. The angular offset between the inner and outer surfaces further ensures that the resulting ultrasonic beams are directed at angles most likely to intercept and reflect from defects of interest, regardless of the specific mounting constraints imposed by the inspection environment.

# Advantages of the Invention

The disclosed control head device offers several advantages over conventional ultrasonic probes used for the inspection of cylindrical welds in nuclear reactor components:

1. Improved acoustic coupling is achieved through the close conformance of the concave inner surface to the curvature of the inspected component, reducing signal loss and improving defect detection sensitivity.

2. The non-zero acute angle between the inner and outer curved surfaces allows for optimized beam steering and incidence angles, improving the probability of detecting defects with varying orientations, including circumferential and axial cracking.

3. The modular array of adjacent emitter-receiver elements permits phased-array operation, enabling electronic beam steering and focusing without the need for mechanical scanning in multiple axes, thereby reducing inspection time.

4. The design accommodates the constraints of confined or difficult-to-access inspection environments, such as the underside of a reactor pressure vessel, by decoupling the orientation of the mounting/support surface from that of the transducer array.

5. The device is adaptable to various diameters of cylindrical components by adjusting the radius of curvature of the concave and convex surfaces, as well as the specific acute angle between them, according to the geometry of the component to be inspected.

# Alternative Embodiments

While the foregoing description refers primarily to the inspection of vessel bottom penetrations in nuclear reactors, it will be understood that the control head device disclosed herein may be adapted for use in the inspection of other cylindrical welded components, including piping welds, nozzle welds, and other curved structures found in nuclear, petrochemical, or other industrial applications where reliable detection of welding defects on curved surfaces is required.

Furthermore, the specific angle formed between the planes of the concave and convex surfaces may be varied according to the particular inspection requirements, including the diameter of the component, the thickness of the weld, and the expected orientation of defects to be detected. Multiple control heads with differing angular configurations may be provided as part of an inspection system to allow for optimized coverage of complex weld geometries.

The number, spacing, and size of the individual ultrasonic emitter-receiver elements may also be varied depending on the desired resolution, coverage area, and frequency range required for a given inspection application, without departing from the scope of the present invention.

# The Definite Article: "The"

The word "the" is one of the most frequently used words in the English language, serving as the definite article. Despite its brevity—just three letters—it plays a crucial grammatical role in nearly every sentence we construct.

## Function and Purpose

"The" is used to indicate that a noun refers to something specific or already known to both the speaker and listener. This distinguishes it from the indefinite articles "a" and "an," which refer to something non-specific or being introduced for the first time. For example:

- "I saw **a** dog" (any dog, unspecified)
- "I saw **the** dog" (a specific dog, likely already mentioned or known)

## Frequency and Importance

Linguistic studies consistently rank "the" as the most common word in written and spoken English. Its ubiquity stems from the constant need to reference specific people, places, objects, and concepts in everyday communication. Without it, English would sound unnatural or overly formal, similar to headline writing or telegraphic speech (e.g., "Dog ran into house" versus "The dog ran into the house").

## Grammatical Rules

Several conventions govern its use:

1. **Unique entities**: "The sun," "the moon," "the president" (when referring to a specific holder of office)
2. **Previously mentioned nouns**: Once introduced, subsequent references often take "the"
3. **Superlatives**: "The best," "the tallest," "the most important"
4. **Specific groups or classes**: "The French," "the elderly"

However, "the" is typically omitted before plural or uncountable nouns used in a general sense ("Coffee is popular" rather than "The coffe is popular") and before most proper nouns (though exceptions exist, such as "the Netherlands" or "the United States").

## A Word Worth Studying

For English language learners, mastering "the" is often considered one of the more challenging aspects of grammar, since many languages either lack articles entirely or use them differently. Its correct usage frequently depends on context, convention, and subtle shades of meaning rather than strict, universal rules—making it a fascinating subject of linguistic study despite its outward simplicity.

# PATENT APPLICATION

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The invention relates to devices for ultrasonic non-destructive testing of welded joints, and more particularly to an apparatus for the ultrasonic examination of welds located on curved walls, such as welds formed at the junction between a nozzle or penetration tube and the curved bottom head of a pressure vessel, for example a nuclear reactor vessel. The invention finds particular application in the in-service inspection of bottom-mounted instrumentation (BMI) penetrations, control rod drive mechanism (CRDM) penetrations, or other tube-to-shell welds formed in the hemispherical or curved bottom head of a nuclear reactor pressure vessel, where access is difficult, radiation levels may be significant, and the geometry of the curved wall complicates the coupling and orientation of conventional ultrasonic transducers relative to the weld to be inspected.

---

## INDEPENDENT CLAIM

**Claim 1.** An ultrasonic testing device for detecting flaws in a weld joining a tubular element to a curved wall of a vessel, the device comprising:

- a support adapted to be positioned against the curved wall in the vicinity of the tubular element, the support having a bearing surface shaped to conform to and bear against the curved wall so as to position the device relative to the weld to be inspected;

- a carriage mounted on the support so as to be movable relative thereto along at least one degree of freedom, so as to permit displacement of the carriage around the tubular element along a path corresponding substantially to the curvature of the wall;

- at least one ultrasonic transducer mounted on the carriage, the transducer being oriented so as to emit an ultrasonic beam toward the weld and to receive ultrasonic echoes reflected from the weld, the transducer being movable relative to the carriage so as to adjust an incidence angle of the ultrasonic beam relative to the curved wall; and

- an orientation adjustment mechanism interposed between the carriage and the transducer, the orientation adjustment mechanism being arranged to modify at least the incidence angle and an azimuthal orientation of the transducer as the carriage is displaced along the curved wall, so as to maintain the ultrasonic beam directed toward the weld notwithstanding variation in the curvature of the wall as the carriage moves around the tubular element.

# ULTRASONIC PROBE ASSEMBLY FOR WELD INSPECTION

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to non-destructive testing apparatus, and more particularly to an ultrasonic probe assembly configured for inspection of welded joints, including but not limited to circumferential and longitudinal welds in pipes, pressure vessels, and other cylindrical or curved structures.

## BACKGROUND

Ultrasonic testing of welded joints typically requires precise coupling between a transducer and the surface of a workpiece to ensure reliable transmission and reception of acoustic energy. Conventional flat-faced probes often exhibit poor acoustic coupling when applied to curved surfaces, such as the exterior or interior surfaces of pipes, tubes, or vessels, resulting in signal loss, inconsistent readings, and reduced defect detection sensitivity. There exists a need for a probe assembly having a contact surface geometry matched to the curvature of the inspected component, while further incorporating multiple transducer elements arranged to insonify a weld region from a plurality of complementary angles.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In one aspect, there is provided an ultrasonic probe assembly comprising a probe body having an inner side and an outer side opposite the inner side, wherein at least one of the inner side and the outer side defines a curved surface configured to conform to a cylindrical surface of a workpiece to be inspected. The probe assembly further comprises an array of ultrasonic transducer elements disposed within or upon the probe body, wherein at least two transducer elements of the array are oriented at an angle relative to one another such that acoustic beams generated thereby are directed toward a weld region of the workpiece along different, non-parallel propagation paths.

In certain embodiments, the inner side comprises a concave curved surface configured to seat against a convex outer diameter of a pipe, and the outer side comprises a convex curved surface, such that the probe body has a curvature substantially corresponding to the curvature of the pipe. In other embodiments, the probe assembly is configured for placement against an interior surface of a cylindrical vessel, wherein the outer side comprises a convex curved surface configured to conform to a concave inner diameter of the vessel.

The angled arrangement of the transducer elements permits generation and reception of ultrasonic shear waves, longitudinal waves, or a combination thereof, at a plurality of incidence angles relative to a weld centerline, thereby enhancing detection of volumetric and planar discontinuities including but not limited to porosity, lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, and cracking, oriented in various directions within the weld and adjacent heat-affected zones.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### General Configuration of the Probe Body

Referring generally to the drawings, an ultrasonic probe assembly 100 is provided comprising a probe body 110 having a first side, referred to herein as an inner side 112, and a second side opposite the inner side, referred to herein as an outer side 114. As used herein, the term "inner side" refers to the side of the probe body 110 intended to be positioned proximate to, and preferably in acoustic contact with, a surface of a workpiece 10 under inspection, while the term "outer side" refers to the side of the probe body 110 opposite the inner side 112, which may face away from the workpiece 10 and may, in certain embodiments, serve as a mounting or handling surface, or may itself be configured to contact a second workpiece surface, as described further below.

The probe body 110 may be fabricated from a rigid or semi-rigid polymer, composite, or metallic material suitable for housing and supporting the transducer array described below, and may further incorporate or be coupled to a wear-resistant coupling layer, wedge, or shoe disposed along the inner side 112 to facilitate acoustic coupling with the workpiece 10.

In accordance with the present disclosure, at least one of the inner side 112 and the outer side 114 defines a curved cylindrical surface 116. In a preferred embodiment, the curved cylindrical surface 116 of the inner side 112 is concave, having a radius of curvature R1 selected to correspond substantially to an outer radius of a pipe, tube, or cylindrical vessel constituting at least a portion of the workpiece 10, such that the inner side 112 seats in conforming surface contact against the exterior of the workpiece 10 when the probe assembly 100 is placed thereon. The outer side 114 may likewise define a curved cylindrical surface having a convex profile, such that the probe body 110, taken in cross-section, exhibits a curved, shell-like or arcuate geometry extending between the inner side 112 and the outer side 114.

It will be appreciated that in alternative embodiments, the curvature of the inner side 112 may be convex, for example where the probe assembly 100 is configured for insertion into and inspection from within a bore, pipe interior, or vessel interior, such that the inner side 112 is configured to contact a concave interior surface of the workpiece 10. In such embodiments, the outer side 114 may define a complementary or independently selected curvature, or may be substantially planar, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

The radius of curvature of the curved cylindrical surface 116 may be fixed, corresponding to a specific pipe diameter or class of pipe diameters, or may be adjustable by way of a flexible or articulated probe body 110, segmented shoe elements, or a compliant coupling membrane disposed along the inner side 112, so as to permit the probe assembly 100 to conform to a range of workpiece diameters.

### Transducer Array and Angular Arrangement

The probe assembly 100 further comprises an array 120 of ultrasonic transducer elements 122a, 122b, ... 122n disposed within the probe body 110, proximate the inner side 112. Each transducer element 122 is configured to generate and/or receive ultrasonic acoustic energy, such as shear waves, longitudinal waves, surface waves, or combinations thereof, and to transmit such energy into the workpiece 10 via the inner side 112, optionally through an intervening coupling wedge, membrane, or couplant layer.

In accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure, at least a first transducer element 122a and a second transducer element 122b of the array 120 are disposed at an angle θ relative to one another, such that a first acoustic beam 130a generated by the first transducer element 122a propagates along a first propagation path non-parallel to a second acoustic beam 130b generated by the second transducer element 122b. The angle θ may be selected within a range of approximately 5 degrees to approximately 80 degrees, and in certain preferred embodiments within a range of approximately 30 degrees to approximately 70 degrees, so as to direct the respective acoustic beams 130a, 130b toward a common weld region 20 of the workpiece 10 from differing incidence angles.

In certain embodiments, the array 120 comprises a plurality of transducer elements 122 arranged in a linear, arcuate, or matrix configuration along the inner side 112, wherein successive transducer elements 122 are incrementally angled relative to one another so as to generate a corresponding plurality of acoustic beams 130 sweeping through a range of incidence angles relative to a centerline of the weld region 20. Such an arrangement permits the probe assembly 100, in a single placement or pass along the workpiece 10, to interrogate the weld region 20 and adjacent heat-affected zones for discontinuities oriented at a variety of angles, including discontinuities oriented substantially parallel to the weld centerline, such as lack-of-fusion defects, and discontinuities oriented transversely thereto, such as certain crack morphologies.

In further embodiments, the transducer elements 122 of the array 120 are individually or collectively coupled to a phased array control system configured to selectively energize the transducer elements 122 in a predetermined sequence and with predetermined relative time delays, so as to electronically steer and/or focus a composite acoustic beam at a plurality of angles and depths within the workpiece 10, in addition to or in lieu of the fixed angular offsets described above.

### Combined Curvature and Angular Beam Configuration

It is a particular feature of the present disclosure that the curved cylindrical surface 116 of the inner side 112, in combination with the angled arrangement of the transducer elements 122 of the array 120, cooperate to maintain substantially consistent acoustic coupling and beam incidence angles across the width of the probe body 110, notwithstanding the curvature of the workpiece 10. In particular, the curvature of the inner side 112 compensates for the curvature of the workpiece surface such that each transducer element 122, despite being positioned at a different location along the curved inner side 112, maintains a substantially consistent standoff distance and coupling angle relative to the local surface of the workpiece 10, thereby preserving the intended angular relationship between the respective acoustic beams 130a, 130b, ... 130n as they converge upon or traverse the weld region 20.

### Additional Embodiments

In certain embodiments, the probe assembly 100 further comprises a housing enclosing the probe body 110 and the transducer array 120, the housing having an aperture or acoustically transparent window aligned with the inner side 112 to permit transmission of the acoustic beams 130 therethrough. In certain embodiments, the probe assembly 100 further comprises position-encoding means, such as an encoder wheel or electromagnetic tracking element, configured to correlate acoustic signal data received by the transducer elements 122 with a position of the probe assembly 100 along the workpiece 10, so as to facilitate generation of a positionally-resolved inspection record of the weld region 20.

It will be understood by those skilled in the art that the specific radii of curvature, angular offsets, number and arrangement of transducer elements, and materials of construction described herein are provided by way of example and not limitation, and that various modifications may be made without departing from the spirit and scope of the present disclosure as defined by the appended claims.

## EXEMPLARY CLAIMS

**1.** An ultrasonic probe assembly for inspection of a welded workpiece, comprising:

counterfactuals.output:
# TECHNICAL FIELD

The present invention relates to a device for the non-destructive testing of mechanical parts, and more particularly to a control head intended for the detection of defects, notably welding defects, in metallic or composite structures by ultrasonic examination.

# BACKGROUND ART

Non-destructive testing methods based on the propagation of ultrasonic waves are widely employed for the inspection of welded joints, in particular in the fields of pressure vessel manufacture, pipeline construction, and aeronautical or nuclear industry components. Such methods generally require a control head comprising at least one emitter transducer and at least one receiver transducer, arranged so as to generate and detect ultrasonic waves propagating within the part to be examined.

However, the control heads known from the prior art present certain drawbacks, notably as regards the detection of defects oriented obliquely with respect to the surface of the part, such as lack-of-fusion defects or crack-type defects situated at the weld bead itself or in the heat-affected zone adjacent thereto.

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The invention aims to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks by providing a control head enabling improved detection of welding defects, in particular of defects oriented at an angle with respect to a main surface of the part under examination.

To this end, the invention relates to a control head for a device for the non-destructive testing of a part, said control head comprising a body extending along a longitudinal axis between a proximal end and a distal end, the proximal end being intended to be connected to a cable or a connector for connection to a processing unit, and the distal end being intended to be brought into contact with, or into proximity to, a surface of the part to be examined.

According to the invention, the control head further comprises at least one emitter-receiver array comprising a plurality of emitter transducers and a plurality of receiver transducers, said array being disposed at the distal end of the body and arranged according to an inclination angle relative to the longitudinal axis of the body, this inclination angle being comprised, preferably, between 30° and 60°.

# DETAILED DESCRIPTION

With reference to the figures, the control head 1 comprises a body 2 extending along a longitudinal axis X-X' between a proximal end 3 and a distal end 4. The proximal end 3 is provided with connection means 5, notably a connector or a cable gland, enabling the control head 1 to be connected to a processing and control unit (not represented) via an electrical cable 6.

The distal end 4 of the body 2 carries an emitter-receiver array 7, disposed according to an inclination angle α with respect to the longitudinal axis X-X' of the body 2. This inclination angle α is preferably comprised between 30° and 60°, and more preferably substantially equal to 45°, so as to optimize the incidence of the ultrasonic waves emitted with respect to the presumed orientation of the welding defects to be detected.

The emitter-receiver array 7 comprises a plurality of emitter transducers 8 and a plurality of receiver transducers 9, arranged in an alternating or interleaved manner along the array 7. Each emitter transducer 8 is configured to generate an ultrasonic wave which propagates within the part 10 to be examined, notably through a weld bead 11 or a heat-affected zone 12 adjacent to the weld bead 11. Each receiver transducer 9 is configured to detect the ultrasonic waves reflected or diffracted by a potential defect 13 present within the part 10.

According to a particular embodiment, the emitter transducers 8 and the receiver transducers 9 are piezoelectric transducers, capable of being excited according to a predetermined excitation sequence so as to generate a focused or steered ultrasonic beam, notably by the phased array technique.

The inclination angle α of the emitter-receiver array 7 relative to the longitudinal axis X-X' of the body 2 advantageously enables the control head 1 to be positioned close to the weld bead 11, while directing the ultrasonic beam according to an angle of incidence favourable to the detection of defects 13 oriented obliquely with respect to the surface 14 of the part 10, notably defects of the lack-of-fusion or crack type situated at the weld bead 11 itself or in the heat-affected zone 12.

According to another embodiment, the control head 1 further comprises coupling means 15, notably a coupling wedge made of a material having an acoustic impedance suited to ensure the transmission of the ultrasonic waves between the emitter-receiver array 7 and the surface 14 of the part 10, said coupling wedge being interposed between the distal end 4 of the body 2 and the surface 14 of the part 10.

According to yet another embodiment, the control head 1 comprises guiding means, notably at least one roller or a sliding shoe, disposed at the distal end 4 of the body 2, so as to enable a displacement of the control head 1 along the weld bead 11, notably in a direction substantially parallel to a longitudinal axis of the weld bead 11.

# ADVANTAGES OF THE INVENTION

The control head according to the invention thus enables an improved detection of welding defects, notably of defects oriented obliquely with respect to the surface of the part under examination, while allowing simplified implementation of the non-destructive testing device, notably by virtue of the arrangement of the emitter-receiver array according to an inclination angle relative to the longitudinal axis of the body of the control head.

# ULTRASONIC INSPECTION APPARATUS FOR CYLINDRICAL NUCLEAR REACTOR COMPONENTS

## Detailed Description of the Probe Head Geometry

**[0001]** In accordance with a preferred embodiment of the present invention, there is provided an ultrasonic inspection apparatus specifically configured for the non-destructive examination of cylindrical nuclear reactor components, including but not limited to reactor pressure vessel welds, control rod drive housings, and steam generator tubing. The apparatus comprises a probe head assembly having a contact face geometrically contoured to conform substantially to the curvature of the cylindrical component under inspection, thereby ensuring consistent acoustic coupling across the entire scanning surface.

**[0002]** The probe head assembly includes an outer casing having a concave curved surface with a radius of curvature R₁ selected to correspond to, or approximate within a tolerance of ±5%, the outer diameter of the cylindrical component to be inspected. Said outer casing defines a longitudinal axis substantially parallel to the longitudinal axis of the cylindrical component during normal operative positioning. The outer casing further comprises a housing wall of substantially uniform thickness t, said thickness being selected within the range of 3 millimeters to 15 millimeters to provide structural rigidity while minimizing acoustic attenuation losses during signal transmission and reception.

**[0003]** Disposed within the outer casing is a transducer element mounted upon a transducer support surface, said transducer support surface being oriented at a predetermined incident angle θ relative to a reference plane defined by the outer casing's inner curved surface at the point of transducer mounting. In a preferred embodiment, the incident angle θ is selected from the range of 0 degrees to 70 degrees, and more preferably from 30 degrees to 45 degrees, to facilitate the generation of shear wave or angled longitudinal wave propagation suitable for detection of circumferentially or axially oriented flaws, including but not limited to stress corrosion cracking and fatigue-induced discontinuities characteristic of said cylindrical reactor components.

**[0004]** The transducer support surface itself defines a second curved contour having a radius of curvature R₂, wherein R₂ is selected independently of R₁ such that the transducer element's active face maintains a substantially constant standoff distance d from the outer casing's inner surface across the width of the transducer element. In certain embodiments, R₂ may be substantially equal to R₁, thereby establishing a concentric relationship between the transducer support surface and the outer casing curvature; in alternative embodiments, R₂ may differ from R₁ by a factor selected to compensate for beam divergence characteristics of the transducer element, said factor being determinable as a function of the transducer's center frequency, element diameter, and the acoustic velocity of the coupling medium disposed between the transducer element and the outer casing.

**[0005]** The angle θ between the plane tangent to the transducer support surface at its center point and the plane tangent to the outer casing's outer curved surface at the corresponding point of nearest approach is maintained within said predetermined range through a mounting bracket or wedge member interposed between the transducer element and the interior surface of the outer casing. Said wedge member may be fabricated from a polymeric material having an acoustic impedance selected to minimize reflection losses at the wedge-casing interface, and may further incorporate one or more internal surfaces configured to attenuate or redirect spurious reflections arising from mode-converted wave components, thereby improving signal-to-noise ratio during inspection of the cylindrical reactor component.

**[0006]** It will be appreciated by persons skilled in the art that the specific values of R₁, R₂, θ, and t recited herein are exemplary and may be varied according to the diameter, wall thickness, and material composition of the particular cylindrical nuclear reactor component under inspection, without departing from the scope and spirit of the present invention as defined by the appended claims.
